title: Foundations of Neural Network Architecture
topics: Introduction to Neural Network Structure for Handwritten Digit Recognition
Introduction to Neural Networks and Neuron Activation
Neural Network Architecture for Digit Recognition
lecture_notes: The lecture introduces the challenge of image recognition, specifically identifying handwritten digits (0-9) represented as 28x28 pixel grids. While human visual cortex processing is highly efficient at invariant recognition—identifying the same digit despite significant pixel-level variation—programmatic implementation of this task is complex. The lecture aims to demystify neural networks by framing them as mathematical structures rather than abstract buzzwords. The core objective is to build a neural network capable of classifying handwritten digits, with the current focus on the structural architecture of the network, leaving the learning process for subsequent discussion.

This lecture introduces the fundamental structure of a basic, 'plain vanilla' neural network. The speaker defines a neuron as a container for a single numerical value, specifically ranging between 0 and 1, referred to as its activation. In the context of image processing, the input layer consists of neurons corresponding to the pixels of an image. For a 28x28 pixel image, the network utilizes 784 input neurons, where each neuron's activation represents the grayscale intensity of the pixel, with 0 representing black and 1 representing white. The lecture emphasizes that while neural networks are inspired by biological brains, their current implementation is a simplified mathematical model. This foundational structure serves as a prerequisite for understanding more complex, modern variants of neural networks.

The network is structured into three main components: an input layer, hidden layers, and an output layer. The input layer consists of 784 neurons, each representing the activation level of a pixel in an image. The output layer contains 10 neurons, each corresponding to a digit (0-9), where activation values between 0 and 1 indicate the system's confidence in the classification. Two hidden layers, each containing 16 neurons, serve as intermediate processing stages. The network functions by propagating activations from one layer to the next, a process loosely modeled on biological neural firing patterns. The specific number of hidden layers and neurons per layer is flexible and often determined experimentally rather than by a fixed rule.
